meta.description: Genuinely Churchill — House of Commons, 4 June 1940, recorded in Hansard. But it is not 'we shall fight THEM on the beaches' (that word isn't in the speech), the famous recording is a 1949 re-recording, and it stays in copyright until 2035.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1874–1965 · British prime minister and Nobel laureate
answer.sourceLine: House of Commons, 4 June 1940, in the ‘War Situation’ debate as the Dunkirk evacuation ended — Hansard, vol 361, cols 795–96. Two things almost everyone gets wrong: the word ‘them’ is not in it (“we shall fight them on the beaches” is a misquotation), and the recording you have heard is not from 1940 — he re-recorded the speech in a studio in 1949.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 4 June 1940, as the Dunkirk evacuation ended
A 1949 studio re-recording, not the 1940 delivery

source.excerpt: We shall go on to the end. We shall fight in France, we shall fight on the seas and oceans, we shall fight with growing confidence and growing strength in the air, we shall defend our island, whatever the cost may be. We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills; we shall never surrender.
trail: Hansard records the peroration in the ‘War Situation’ debate of 4 June 1940, in the sequence France → seas and oceans → air → island → beaches → landing grounds → fields and streets → hills → never surrender Hansard, HC Deb 4 Jun 1940 ↗.

There is no ‘them’ anywhere in it. The ubiquitous ‘we shall fight them on the beaches’ — common in films and advertising — inserts a word Churchill did not use, and slightly changes the sense from defending ground to engaging an enemy.

The audio everyone knows is a 1949 studio re-recording. Churchill did not broadcast this speech live on 4 June 1940, so clips captioned as 1940 recordings are mis-dated — a useful check when a ‘contemporary recording’ is offered as evidence.
source.excerptNote: The peroration as Hansard records it. Note the full sequence — reproductions routinely drop ‘in the fields and in the streets’ or reorder the hills and streets.

author.heading: About Winston Churchill
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British prime minister, statesman & Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Sir Winston Churchill led Britain through the Second World War and won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature for his historical writing and oratory. He delivered this three weeks into his premiership, as the last troops came off the Dunkirk beaches and invasion looked imminent. It is among the most quoted passages in the language — and, unlike much of what is pinned on him, entirely and verifiably his.

misattribution.heading: Correctly credited — but routinely misquoted
misattribution.intro: Nobody doubts who said this. It is nonetheless one of the most consistently misquoted passages in English, and the most common error changes the meaning.

items.why: ‘Them’ appears nowhere in the speech. Churchill names places, not an enemy — the force of the passage is the list of ground to be defended. The inserted word is extremely common in films and advertising Hansard ↗.

items.who: ‘in the fields and in the streets’
items.why: Frequently omitted, and the hills and streets are often swapped. ‘Landing grounds’ is regularly rendered ‘landing fields,’ and ‘on the seas and oceans’ as ‘in the oceans.’
The familiar audio is a 1949 studio re-recording; the speech was not broadcast live on 4 June 1940. Clips captioned as contemporaneous 1940 audio are mis-dated.
The much-loved story that he muttered a coda about fighting with broken bottles ‘because that’s bloody well all we’ve got’ is not in Hansard and rests on anecdote. Treat it as unverified.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Churchill, House of Commons, 4 June 1940, recorded in Hansard — without the word ‘them,’ and still in copyright until 2035 official record ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: He was reporting a defeat. Dunkirk had just evacuated over 300,000 men who had left their equipment behind, and the peroration answers the obvious question — what happens when they come — by naming, in order, every kind of ground on which Britain would be fought over.

The repetition is doing the work: each ‘we shall fight’ moves the imagined battle further inland, from the seas to the beaches to the streets to the hills, and the sentence only stops at ‘we shall never surrender.’
detailsBody: ‘We shall fight in France, we shall fight on the seas and oceans…’
‘…we shall fight with growing confidence and growing strength in the air, we shall defend our island, whatever the cost may be.’
‘We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills…’
context.pull: There is no "them" in it. He named places, not an enemy.
